# Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0502a)

**ID:** Atk S0502a
**Section:** Aṭṭhakathā Khuddakanikāya (atk-s05)
**Collection:** Atthakatha-Suttas
**Title (Pali):** Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā
**Title (English, from literature):** Commentary on the Dhammapada
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* is the extensive prose commentary on the verses of the canonical *Dhammapada* within the Khuddakanikāya [Berkwitz 2008; Norman 1983]. Traditionally attributed to Buddhaghosa or an author active in fifth-century Sri Lanka, its colophon states that the work was translated and adapted into the classical Pali language from older Sinhala commentarial traditions (*porāṇatthakathā*) that had been preserved on the island [Collett 2014; Norman 1983]. Rather than an original composition, modern scholarship notes that the commentator performed primarily an editorial role, adapting previously circulating narrative cycles to provide the background settings (*vatthu*) and word-for-word glosses for the verses [Appleton 2014; Norman 1983]. The work contains 267 distinct narrative stories (*vatthu*), including accounts such as the *Garahadinna-vatthu* (commenting on verses 58–59), the story of King Bimbisāra's transference of merit to *peta*s (Dhp-a I 103–104), and the life of Jotika [Appleton 2010; Appleton 2014; Berkwitz 2008; Langer 2007]. Its biographical narratives of early Buddhist figures served as a key source for subsequent commentarial works; for example, Dhammapāla's *Paramatthadīpanī* draws closely upon the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Manorathapūraṇī* for the biographies of major elders in the *Thera-* and *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [Norman 1983; Collett 2014]. In the tenth century, the text was explicated in Sri Lanka by the Sinhala glossary *Dhampiyā Aṭuvā Gäṭapadaya*, and it later inspired Dharmasena Thera's thirteenth-century Sinhala transformation, the *Saddharmaratnāvaliya* [Collett 2014; Endo 1997].

In Southeast Asian manuscript cultures—including Laos, Northern Thailand, and Cambodia—the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* circulated extensively, often copied as selections of popular individual tales rather than as a single immense codex [Berkwitz 2008]. Monastic students commonly used bilingual or annotated manuscripts written in Khom script featuring *tvā kṣien* interlinear glossing systems to facilitate vernacular translation and study [Walker 2018]. In modern scholarship, the text was edited for the Pali Text Society and translated into English by Eugene Watson Burlingame [Walker 2018].

Textual parallels and cross-tradition alignments illustrate widespread reuse of the commentary's narrative material. Prajñāvarman's commentary on the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* cites alternate *nidāna*s that share a common ancestral tradition with the Pali *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Skilling 1993]. In Pali-internal text reuse, DharmaNexus detects 96,817 matching passages across 513 texts, exhibiting massive narrative overlap with the various divisions of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (over 27,000 matches), the *Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Aṅguttaranikāya* commentary (*Manorathapūraṇī*), the *Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*, and Dhammapāla's *Theragāthā-* and *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus; Norman 1983].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Tatiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a3) (§259_1–260_0 ↔ §4339_2–4340_0); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Paṭhamo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a1) (§1060–1068_4 ↔ §2136_0–2144_5); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§3984–3991 ↔ §2660_0–2665); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§1029_11–1038_3 ↔ §1410_2–1417_3); Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0510a) (§1596_1–1603_5 ↔ §3410_0–3420_5); Aṅguttaranikāye Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0401a) (§366_1–380_3 ↔ §582_0–601_3); Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Pañcamo bhāgo) (Atk S0514a1) (§2999_0–3000_7 ↔ §4131_1–4132_8); Petavatthu-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0507a) (§188–201 ↔ §2802–2812)

- [Appleton 2014] Naomi Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth: Buddhist and Jain Multi-life Stories (2014) — Discusses the dating of Dhp-a narratives and the Garahadinna-vatthu
- [Berkwitz 2008] Stephen C. Berkwitz, Juliane Schober, Claudia Brown, eds., Buddhist Manuscript Cultures (2008) — Reports the text length (267 stories) and its manuscript circulation in Laos and Northern Thailand
- [Collett 2014] Alice Collett, ed., Women in Early Indian Buddhism: Comparative Textual Studies (2014) — Details on the colophon, translation from Old Sinhala, Buddhaghosa, and the Saddharmaratnāvaliya
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus Database — Automated text-reuse statistics with Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā, and others
- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism (1997/2002) — Mentions the 10th-century Sinhala glossary Dhampiyā Aṭuvā Gäṭapadaya and Dhp-a phraseology
- [Langer 2007] Rita Langer, Buddhist Rituals of Death and Rebirth: Contemporary Sri Lankan Practice and Its Origins (2007) — Discusses the Bimbisāra story and merit transference in Dhp-a I 103–4
